https://www.politico.eu/article/iran-str.text: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi Friday said his country is offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days and resume talks on its nuclear program in exchange for concessions from Washington. Those would include lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waiving sanctions on Iranian oil sales and a ceasefire that would include Lebanon, Araghchi told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, according to an AP report . “The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he said on Friday, adding that Iran had conveyed its offer to the U.S. through Qatar. Although U.S. President Donald Trump has not formally responded to the proposal, he privately rejected the plan, according to a Wall Street Journal report citing U.S. officials. He is instead betting on renewed escalation including by raising the possibility of another bombing campaign on the country after the midterm elections in November, according to the same report. Trump on Friday night shared a map of the region on Truth Social, renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the “Trump Strait.” The Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for global oil and natural gas supplies and has been a major flashpoint since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran in February. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: The sifting of who gets on a migrant dinghy bound for the UK is in the hands of criminal gangs, according to Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary. Photograph: Yoan Valat/EPA View image in fullscreen The sifting of who gets on a migrant dinghy bound for the UK is in the hands of criminal gangs, according to Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary. Photograph: Yoan Valat/EPA Immigration and asylum Nearly all women arriving on small boats have been raped, says Shabana Mahmood Home secretary warns people traffickers will exploit asylum seekers because they decide who comes to the UK Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Sun 4 Oct 2026 14.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nearly all women who try to reach the UK in small boats from northern France have been raped on their journey, Shabana Mahmood has claimed. In an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast, the home secretary said far-right, balaclava-wearing activists would “kill” or “kick me out of my own country” if they took power. Speaking to the former Tory minister Rory Stewart and Tony Blair’s former close adviser Alastair Campbell, she said sexual abusers would exploit most asylum seekers as long as traffickers continued to decide who came to the UK. She said: “We’re not in control of this border. The sifting of the people that end up in the north of France and are about to get on a dinghy is done by criminal gangs who are also, by the way, people traffickers. “You can almost guarantee that every woman that’s in the north of France has probably been raped along the journey. Some of the men too, they’ve certainly been abused and threatened. That is not the model that should decide whether somebody gets to come to the UK, make this their place of sanctuary and ultimately become one of us.” View image in fullscreen Shabana Mahmood said she was ‘very uncomfortable’ about the arrests of 82 people at the Labour conference for displaying articles in support of Palestine Action. Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/Shutterstock Asked by Campbell about balaclava-wearing protesters shutting down ports and praising her policies, she said they should “sod off”. She added: “They’re just troublemakers. You know, they’d kill me in a minute if they could, and they’d definitely kick me out of my own country. So let’s just be really clear about who and what they are. They don’t think I’m a true Brit and they hate the fact that I’m a Muslim.” Mahmood also said she considered herself “part of the pro-Palestinian cause” and felt “very uncomfortable” over the arrests of activists opposing the ban imposed on Palestine Action. Merseyside police arrested 82 people on Monday at the Labour party conference on suspicion of wearing or carrying articles supporting a proscribed organisation. In a protest organised by Defend Our Juries, scores of people sat outside the conference centre in Liverpool, many holding handmade banners saying they supported Palestine Action. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Shabana Mahmood said far-right thugs ‘would kill me in a minute if they could’. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA Mahmood said: “For those of us who have been in the pro-Palestinian cause all of our lives, these are people – sometimes you’ll know who they are, you know, you’ve been on the marches with them – it feels very uncomfortable to see them falling foul of section 13 of the Terrorism Act.” However, she defended enforcing the ban, regardless of her views: “You’ve got to be able to apply your principles, even when it’s uncomfortable for you, because you’re going to really want to apply them when it’s something you, you know, with your whole heart, are feeling very passionately about.” Authorities were preparing on Sunday for the arrival of a migrant dinghy heading for the south coast. The boat was being shadowed by French coastguard and rescue vessels and moving toward the Channel boundary line, according to ship tracking data. It appeared to have set off from near the Utah Beach area of Normandy on Sunday morning. Caroline Dinenage, the Conservative MP for Gosport in Hampshire, said there was “nothing to suggest” the boat would land on the county’s coast but police were “making preparations should that situation change”. A government spokesperson said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border. It is vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.” Imran Hussain, a director at the Refugee Council, welcomed the home secretary’s acknowledgment of widespread sexual violence, but questioned why the government had closed safe and legal routes which could help asylum seekers avoid falling into the hands of predators. “We know from our services that women and girls fleeing war and persecution face sexual violence both in the conflicts they have escaped and on the journeys they are forced to make in search of safety,” he said. “That is why in welcoming the government’s announcement last week of new safe routes we called for them not to be limited to a few hundred people. Last year the government closed family reunion, the safe route for refugees which overwhelmingly benefits women and children. “It is entirely right to talk about the dangers women face on these journeys but we should not be closing the safe routes that could keep them out of harm’s way. Protecting women means more safe routes, not fewer.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Refugees Violence against women and girls Shabana Mahmood Rape and sexual assault Labour news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Why is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped? https://www.dw.com/en/students-list-cand.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PXdG Prefer DW on Google The Students' List has pledged many reforms in domestic politics Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule. The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's new government. The movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties. Serbia's student-led movement ends Vucic era To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade , to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience. Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance. According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat. 90 days to form a government The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed. Lessons from Serbia: how students defeated an authoritarian leader To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with. They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms. The election of a new parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister. A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27. Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.
